title: Discounted Cash Flow and Where the Value Actually Sits
summary: Five years of detailed forecasting produced a fifth of the answer — the rest came from two assumptions on one line.

lesson.body:
A [[dcf|discounted cash flow]] valuation says something simple: **a business is worth the cash it will produce, discounted for the fact that the cash arrives later and may not arrive at all.**

Three components, and the third is where the trouble lives:

**Explicit forecast.** Cash flows modelled year by year, usually five to ten years. The part everyone spends their time on.

**[[terminal-value|Terminal value]].** Everything after the forecast horizon, collapsed into one number at the end of it.

**[[discount-rate|Discount rate]].** Usually [[wacc|WACC]] for cash flows to the whole firm, or the cost of equity for cash flows to shareholders. Getting this wrong invalidates everything above it.

One consistency rule matters more than any refinement: **match the cash flow to the discount rate.** [[free-cash-flow|Free cash flow]] to the firm — before interest — is discounted at WACC and gives [[enterprise-value|enterprise value]]. Free cash flow to equity — after interest — is discounted at the cost of equity and gives equity value directly. **Mixing them is the single most common structural error in a valuation model**, and it usually flatters the answer.

Subtract [[net-debt|net debt]] from enterprise value to reach equity value. That bridge is where a leveraged company's valuation gets interesting.

**Most of a DCF's answer comes from the terminal value, which is the part with the least analysis behind it.**

The usual construction is a [[perpetuity]]: take the final forecast year's cash flow, grow it forever at a constant rate, and divide by the discount rate minus that growth rate.

Two numbers therefore carry most of the valuation: **the discount rate and the perpetual growth rate.** And they enter as a *difference* in the denominator, which makes the result violently sensitive to both. At an 8% discount rate, moving perpetual growth from 2% to 3% changes the denominator from 6% to 5% — a 20% change in the divisor from a one-point change in an assumption nobody can verify.

Two disciplines follow, and they are not optional:

**Perpetual growth cannot exceed long-run economic growth.** A business growing faster than the economy forever eventually becomes the economy. Anything above [[nominal-gdp|nominal GDP]] growth is an arithmetic impossibility rather than an aggressive assumption.

**Cross-check the terminal value against an exit multiple.** Divide it by the final year's [[ebitda|EBITDA]]. If the answer implies a multiple far above what the business would actually trade at, the perpetuity assumptions are doing something the market would not.

**A DCF is not a precision instrument. It is a framework for making assumptions explicit** — and its main value is that it forces you to state what you believe about growth, margins and the cost of capital, where a multiple lets you avoid saying.

**The single number a DCF produces is the least useful thing it produces. The sensitivity table is the output.**

In the worked example below, plausible ranges on two assumptions — a percentage point either way on the discount rate and on perpetual growth — produce a valuation range from 26% below the base case to 62% above it.

That is not a defect in the method. **It is the honest width of what can be known about a business's value**, and any single figure quoted to the nearest million is concealing it.

So the practical use of a DCF inverts the usual presentation:

**Run it backwards.** Instead of asking what the business is worth, ask what has to be true to justify the current price. What growth rate, what margin, what discount rate? Then argue about whether those are plausible. This is a far more productive conversation than comparing two point estimates.

**Report the range and the drivers.** "Between 1,700 and 3,800 depending mostly on the cost of capital" is more useful and more honest than 2,349.

**Use it to find the disagreement.** When two people value the same business differently, the DCF locates exactly which assumption they differ on — and that is usually a question with evidence attached, where "it's worth more than that" is not.

lesson.plainReading: Terminal value at the end of the forecast is next year's cash flow divided by the discount rate minus the perpetual growth rate. Because the two rates appear as a difference, small changes in either move the answer a great deal.

variables.meaning: free cash flow in the final explicit forecast year
perpetual growth rate — cannot exceed long-run nominal economic growth
the [[discount-rate|discount rate]], matched to the cash flow definition

lesson.body: A business generating 100 of free cash flow, growing 6% a year for five years, then 3% forever. Discount rate 8%.
walkthrough: [[present-value|Present value]] of those five years, discounted at 8%: **472.9**.
**Read that carefully: 79.9% of the value came from the terminal calculation. Five years of detailed forecasting produced a fifth of the answer.**
Now the sensitivity. At a 9% discount rate and 2% growth: **1,728**. At 7% and 4%: **3,794**. The same business, plausible assumptions, a range of **−26% to +62%**.

And the cross-check: if year-5 EBITDA is 180, a terminal value of 2,757 implies an exit multiple of **15.3x**. Is that what this business would trade at? If comparable companies change hands at 9x, the perpetuity assumptions are asserting something the market does not.

Sanity check worth reusing: **compute the terminal value's share of the total, and convert the terminal value into an implied exit multiple.** Two numbers, and together they tell you whether you have built a valuation or an assumption with a spreadsheet wrapped around it.

lesson.caption: Enterprise value at different discount and growth rates

lesson.body:
**Perpetual growth above nominal GDP growth.** The business eventually becomes larger than the economy. It is not aggressive, it is impossible, and it appears in models regularly.

**Mismatched cash flows and discount rates.** Discounting cash flow to equity at WACC, or firm cash flow at the cost of equity. Both produce a plausible-looking number that means nothing.

**Forecast periods extended to hide the terminal value.** Ten years of explicit forecast reduces the terminal share — and years six to ten are not forecasts, they are the terminal assumption written out longhand.

**Sensitivity tables that vary only what does not matter.** Flexing revenue growth by 1% while holding the discount rate fixed produces a comfortingly narrow range and tests nothing.

**A discount rate reverse-engineered from the answer.** Once a target price exists, the discount rate becomes the plug. This is common, invisible in the output, and detectable by asking how the discount rate was derived before the model was built.

**The most useful way to run a DCF is backwards, and almost nobody does it.**

Instead of forecasting cash flows to produce a value, take the observed price and solve for the assumptions that justify it. What perpetual growth rate does this price imply? What margin? What return on capital?

The advantage is that it converts an unfalsifiable exercise into a testable one. "This business is worth 2,349" invites disagreement with no resolution. **"This price implies 4% perpetual growth and margins expanding 300bp" invites a specific argument about whether either is likely** — and both are questions with evidence attached.

It is particularly useful in two situations an alternatives analyst meets constantly.

**Assessing an entry price.** What does the sponsor's model need to believe? If it needs above-market growth *and* margin expansion *and* multiple expansion, those are three bets, not one, and they need to be sized as three.

**Assessing a mark.** A portfolio company held at 12x when comparable transactions clear at 9x is a claim. Reverse the valuation and the claim becomes specific: this mark requires the business to be worth a third more than its peers, and here is the reason offered.

**The general principle: a valuation you cannot argue with is a valuation nobody has tested.**

**Ask what share of the valuation is terminal value.** Above about 70% — which is most models — the analysis is mostly about two assumptions, and the explicit forecast is decoration.

**Convert the terminal value into an implied exit multiple and compare with comparable transactions.** It is a one-line check and it catches unrealistic perpetuity assumptions immediately.

**Ask for the sensitivity table on the discount rate and perpetual growth together.** Varying one at a time understates the range badly.

**Run it backwards on any price you are being asked to pay.** What growth and margin does this price require? Then argue about those rather than about the valuation.

**Ask how the discount rate was derived, and when.** A rate set before the model was built is an input; a rate that appeared afterwards is a plug.

items: In the worked example 79.9% of the enterprise value came from the terminal calculation — five years of detailed forecasting produced a fifth of the answer.
Discount rate and perpetual growth enter as a difference, so a point either way on both moved the value from −26% to +62% of the base case.
Always convert the terminal value into an implied exit multiple: 2,757 on year-5 EBITDA of 180 is 15.3x, which is a claim comparable transactions can test.
Run the DCF backwards. "This price implies 4% perpetual growth and 300bp of margin expansion" is arguable; "it is worth 2,349" is not.

questions.stem: A discounted cash flow valuation has three components. Which one usually contributes most of the answer?
choices: The explicit year-by-year forecast, since it is the most detailed
The terminal value, which collapses everything after the forecast horizon into one number
The discount rate, which is applied uniformly
rationales: It receives most of the effort and typically produces about a fifth of the value.
Correct. For a growing business at ordinary discount rates the terminal value is commonly 70-80% of the total — which is why the two assumptions behind it deserve most of the scrutiny.
The discount rate is critical and it is an input rather than a component of the value.
Net debt bridges enterprise value to equity value; it does not create the enterprise value.
questions.explanation: Knowing this before opening a model changes where you look first. The five detailed forecast years are usually the part everyone argues about and the smallest part of the answer.

questions.stem: Year-5 free cash flow is 133.8, perpetual growth 3%, discount rate 8%. What is the terminal value at year 5? Round to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation: Note the denominator is 5%, not 8%. That subtraction is what makes terminal values so sensitive: at 2% growth the denominator is 6% and the terminal value drops by a sixth, from one point of change in an assumption about the year 2050.

questions.stem: Present value of the explicit forecast is 472.9 and the present value of the terminal value is 1,876.2. What percentage of enterprise value is terminal? One decimal place.
questions.explanation: Around 80% is entirely typical for a growing business at these rates. It is worth stating out loud in any valuation discussion, because it tells everyone in the room which assumptions the argument should actually be about.

questions.stem: You are discounting free cash flow to the firm — cash flow before interest. Which discount rate is correct?
choices: The cost of equity, because equity holders own the business
WACC, because the cash flow is available to all capital providers
The risk-free rate plus a fixed premium
rationales: The cost of equity matches cash flow to equity, which is measured after interest. Using it here double-counts the benefit of leverage.
Correct. Cash flow before interest belongs to lenders and shareholders together, so it must be discounted at their blended required return, giving enterprise value.
That is one component of WACC and it prices only the debt claim.
This is a way of estimating a discount rate rather than a rule for which one to use.
questions.explanation: The consistency rule is worth stating as a habit: before discounting anything, ask whose cash flow this is. Firm cash flow with WACC gives enterprise value; equity cash flow with the cost of equity gives equity value directly. Mixing them usually flatters the answer, which is why the error survives review.

questions.stem: "We used a 4.5% perpetual growth rate because the company has been growing 15% a year." True or false as a justification — and why?
justifications: False — perpetual growth cannot exceed long-run nominal economic growth, or the business eventually becomes larger than the economy
False — perpetual growth should always be set to zero
True — historical growth is the best guide to perpetual growth
False — because 4.5% is too low for a company growing at 15%
rationales: Correct. "Perpetual" means forever, and any rate above the economy's growth implies the firm eventually exceeds the whole economy. Recent growth is evidence about the explicit forecast period, not about eternity.
Zero is a legitimate conservative choice and is not required — inflation alone justifies a positive nominal rate.
Historical growth informs the forecast years; it says nothing about a steady state decades out.
The direction of the objection is reversed: 4.5% is likely too high, not too low.
questions.explanation: The clean way to reason about it: perpetual growth is a statement about a mature business in a mature market, no matter how exciting the company is today. Fast growth belongs in the explicit forecast, and the terminal rate belongs near long-run nominal GDP.

questions.stem: A sponsor's model shows a 22% IRR. What is the most productive way to test it?
choices: Rebuild the model independently with your own assumptions
Solve for what the model requires — growth, margin and exit multiple — and assess whether each is plausible on its own
Compare the IRR with the sponsor's previous funds
Ask for a longer forecast period
rationales: A duplicate model produces a competing number and no resolution — you end up comparing two sets of assumptions without examining either.

Correct. Decomposing the return into its required conditions turns an argument about a figure into several specific arguments with evidence attached. It also reveals when a case needs three favourable things simultaneously.
Track record is relevant context and does not test this deal's assumptions.
A longer forecast expands the same assumptions rather than testing them.
questions.explanation: The decomposition also exposes compounding optimism, which is the common failure: growth above market plus margin expansion plus multiple expansion may each be defensible alone, and requiring all three simultaneously is a much stronger claim than any of them.

questions.stem: A model uses a ten-year explicit forecast rather than five, reducing the terminal share from 80% to 55%. What has actually changed?
choices: The valuation is now more reliable, since more of it is explicitly forecast
Very little — years six to ten are the terminal assumption written out longhand, and the uncertainty has been redistributed rather than reduced
The discount rate must now be higher
The terminal growth rate becomes irrelevant
rationales: Nobody forecasts year nine with meaningful accuracy. The appearance of detail is not the same as knowledge.

Correct. The later forecast years are extrapolations driven by the same steady-state assumptions. Moving value out of the terminal line makes the model look better without changing what it depends on.
The discount rate is unaffected by the length of the forecast horizon.
It still governs everything after year ten, and the intervening years now carry similar assumptions.
questions.explanation: A useful counter-check: ask what year eight's assumptions are and where they came from. If the answer is "it grows with the trend", that is the terminal assumption, and the honest presentation would be a shorter forecast with a clearly labelled terminal value.
